## The four o’clock toast

I did my last night shift on Saturday. Nine at night until half past seven on Sunday morning, in majors. Fourteen years of nights, and then I handed over and went home.

I have been trying to write that sentence since Sunday. I have also been trying to write something here since the spring, so perhaps we shouldn’t expect miracles. Every attempt so far has turned into either a eulogy for night work or a complaint about the NHS. I don’t want to write either of those. I am still going to work. Nobody needs to put my stethoscope on a cushion.

From Monday, I’m on a days-only rota.

My knees are in favour. My sleep, such as it is, is in favour. My GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is no longer something we can discuss in the tone of two people talking about somebody else’s problem. There are good reasons for this change. I wanted it. I am relieved.

I hadn’t expected to feel quite so disloyal.

***

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. I don’t remember very much about the shift itself. I remember being frightened of missing something, and then frightened that someone would notice how frightened I was.

From that first winter, I remember standing in the car park at the Infirmary, crying because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose.

I had. That was established. Nothing had been missed. But by then I had frightened myself beyond the reach of the answer, and I stood beside the car for a while before I could drive.

There was frost on the windscreen. I remember that more clearly than almost anything else: having to scrape it off, the small practical job that still needed doing while I was in such a state.

I would like to say I eventually became a doctor who never felt like that again. I became a doctor who checked things, asked for help and understood that a feeling of dread was not, on its own, proof that I had done something wrong. Mostly, that helped.

Fourteen years is a long time to spend learning how your own brain behaves when it would very much like to be asleep.

***

People who haven’t worked nights sometimes imagine they are all adrenaline. There is some of that, of course. But a great deal of night work is much quieter and harder to describe.

It is explaining something again because the person in front of you is frightened and didn’t take it in the first time. It is noticing that someone is cold. It is trying not to let the tiredness in your voice sound like irritation, especially when, if you are honest, some of it is irritation.

Mostly, it is about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

I have not always managed it. There have been mornings when I have driven home remembering an unnecessarily sharp answer, or realising that I hurried a conversation which mattered more to the other person than it seemed to matter to me. Tiredness explains some things. It doesn’t make them feel better afterwards.

But I have watched other people do this well, over and over again, and learned from them.

Our night charge nurse, Folasade, has been doing nights for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs. I would prefer to attribute this entirely to my knees, but that would not be an honest account.

There is a particular relief in working with someone who knows what needs doing and will tell you. At night, when your judgement feels a little less reliable than it did six hours earlier, that matters enormously.

I will miss working with her. I will miss the people who can tell, from a fairly ordinary “Are you all right?”, whether you mean it as a greeting or whether you need them to stop for a minute.

***

I have always thought the department is most itself at night.

There are fewer managers about, certainly, but that isn’t the whole of it. People are often more direct. There is less energy available for pretending. You can say you are struggling, or that you don’t know, and someone will usually help you get on with the next thing.

There is a lot of kindness. Not grand kindness, generally. Someone finding you a chair. Someone taking over a conversation because they can hear you have run out of patience. Being told to go and eat something.

And at four in the morning, somebody makes toast.

Nobody admits to starting it. You become aware of the smell, and then there is toast in the staff room. I have never established whether there is an informal rota, an instinct shared by certain members of staff, or simply one person who has been doing it for years and would rather not be thanked.

Sometimes you get to eat it while it is hot. Sometimes you don’t. Either way, someone has remembered that people need feeding.

I don’t want to make night shifts sound like a lovely club with occasional medical interruptions. They can be miserable. They are hard on the body, and hard on the people who live around your sleeping. There are shifts you get through and have no wish to discuss afterwards.

But the toast belongs in an honest account too.

***

So does the hand I still think about.

A patient once held mine and told me I had his daughter’s hands. We stayed like that for a little while.

He went home afterwards. I’m glad I know that.

There is no further story I need to tell about him here. He had his own life, and I was briefly in it. But I have remembered what he said, long after forgetting much of the work around it.

***

My sister reads this in Bangalore, when there is anything here to read.

I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies, even over video, because of nights. My sister never once complained. I sometimes think that made it easier for me not to examine how much I minded.

There is always a rota, always a reason, always the possibility of catching up afterwards. You can be sent photographs. Someone can tell you what happened. The children grow up knowing you anyway.

Still, I wanted to be there.

Nights took things I knew I was giving them, and some things I only noticed later. Sleep became something to arrange everything else around, with mixed success. There were days off on which I was technically available but not much use to anyone. I got used to saying, “I’m coming off nights,” as though that explained everything, which sometimes it did.

I don’t regret fourteen years of this work. I do regret some of what I missed. I’m trying to allow both of those statements to stand without making one cancel out the other.

At forty-two, I also have to accept that wanting to carry on doing something is not the same as being able to carry on doing it without consequences. My GP has been particularly helpful on this point. By helpful, I mean firm.

***

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the shipping forecast on catch-up.

The sun was coming up. I have seen that light so many times on the way home: tired, hungry, occasionally still turning some part of the shift over in my head. Sometimes all I have wanted is for the traffic to move so I can get into bed.

This time I realised I wouldn’t see it from this side again.

I will still be awake at sunrise occasionally. I will still drive down the London Road. But I won’t be making that particular journey, out of the department’s night and into everyone else’s morning.

I felt sad about it. Then I thought about being able to sleep at night, regularly, and felt relieved. Then I felt guilty about the relief, which was a fairly exhausting sequence of emotions for someone who had just finished a night shift.

The colleagues staying on nights haven’t accused me of anything. The sense of betrayal appears to be entirely my own contribution. I expect it will settle.

There will be things to learn about days. There will be evenings when I can say yes to something without first doing calculations. I might even write here again before another season has passed.

For now, I am glad I did those years, and glad I don’t have to do the next ones.

I hope Folasade gets a proper break on her next shift. I hope whoever makes the toast makes enough for her, and that she gets to it while it’s hot.
